notes:
Task and constraints: Apply replacement operations at original indices when the source substring matches, producing one final string.
Idea: Precompute valid operations at each original index, then scan the original string once.
Technique and why it applies: bucket stores replacement length and target characters only when the original source matches. The scan emits replacement characters and skips the replaced source span, otherwise copying the original character.
Invariant: i is an index in the original S and result contains output for the original prefix before i.
Edge cases: Overlapping operations at the same index overwrite each other in bucket. The bounds test checks source characters only while each position remains inside S.
Complexity: Validation is O(total source lengths), and the scan is O(n+output length); storage is O(n+output).

Task and constraints: For every tree node, return the sum of distances from that node to all other nodes.
Idea: Run postorder DFS to compute subtree sizes and root distances, then preorder DFS to reroot the distance totals.
Technique and why it applies: Moving the root across an edge decreases distances to the child's subtree by its size and increases distances to all remaining nodes by n-subtree_size.
Invariant: tree_nodes[v] is subtree size; distances[v] first stores the subtree distance sum and is later replaced with the whole-tree sum.
Edge cases: The tree is rooted at node zero and assumed connected. Recursive DFS may exceed Python's recursion limit on a highly skewed tree.
Complexity: Each edge is visited a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(n) storage.

Task and constraints: Compute the sum of distances from every node to all other nodes in a tree.
Idea: Use two DFS passes: aggregate subtree sizes and distances, then reroot results from parent to child.
Technique and why it applies: For child nei, result[nei] equals result[node]-count[nei]+N-count[nei], accounting for distances shortening inside its subtree and lengthening outside.
Invariant: count[v] is the size of v's subtree and result[v] holds the distance sum for the current root.
Edge cases: The code assumes N is positive and the input is a tree. Recursion depth can be O(N) for a chain.
Complexity: Two graph traversals are O(N) time and the adjacency lists and arrays use O(N) space.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of overlapping one-cells when one binary image is translated over another.
Idea: Record coordinates of ones in each image and count every relative shift between a one from each image.
Technique and why it applies: Each coordinate pair votes for the translation that aligns those two ones. The most frequent displacement maximizes overlap.
Invariant: shiftDict[(dx,dy)] counts pairs of one-cells aligned by that translation.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used without an import in the snippet. The code assumes square images because n is derived from img1 and used for both row and column bounds.
Complexity: If images have p and q ones, time is O(n²+p q) and space is O(pq) in the worst case.

Task and constraints: Compute the maximum overlap between two binary square images under translation.
Idea: Count all translations that align each one-cell of A with each one-cell of B.
Technique and why it applies: A translation is encoded as an offset in a flat array; every pair of ones increments the corresponding offset count.
Invariant: count[offset] is the number of aligned one-cell pairs for that translation.
Edge cases: The method assumes both inputs are square and have the same dimensions. With no ones in either image, all counts remain zero and max(count) returns zero.
Complexity: For p and q ones, time is O(pq+n²) due to initialization and pair enumeration; space is O(n²).

Task and constraints: Determine whether two axis-aligned rectangles overlap with positive area.
Idea: Reject the pair if one rectangle lies entirely above, below, left, or right of the other.
Technique and why it applies: Positive-area overlap requires strict intersection along both axes; touching edges alone is not overlap.
Invariant: Each disjunction tests one separating-axis condition.
Edge cases: Equality at a boundary returns False, matching the positive-area requirement. The code assumes rectangle coordinates are given in [x1,y1,x2,y2] order.
Complexity: Only four comparisons are needed, so time and auxiliary space are O(1).

Task and constraints: Check whether two axis-aligned rectangles share a positive-area region.
Idea: Test for a strict interval intersection on both the horizontal and vertical axes.
Technique and why it applies: max(left endpoints) must be strictly less than min(right endpoints) for overlap on an axis; both axes must overlap.
Invariant: intersect returns whether the two intervals overlap with positive length.
Edge cases: Rectangles touching only at an edge or corner are not counted as overlapping. Coordinate ordering is assumed valid.
Complexity: A fixed number of comparisons gives O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the probability that a player finishes with at most n points in the New 21 Game.
Idea: Use a sliding window of probabilities for scores from k through k+maxPts-1, then calculate earlier states backward.
Technique and why it applies: A score below k draws a uniform next value from 1 through maxPts, so its win probability is the average of the next maxPts states. The deque sum is updated as the window shifts.
Invariant: dp's leftmost value is the probability for the current score, and s is the sum of the window probabilities.
Edge cases: collections is used without import. For k=0, initialization and return still follow the code's array setup but deserve testing against the direct probability of already having stopped.
Complexity: O(k+maxPts) time and O(maxPts) deque space.

Task and constraints: Simulate dominoes falling left or right until all forces settle.
Idea: Use breadth-first propagation in rounds, recording net directional influence on each domino.
Technique and why it applies: L pushes its left neighbor and R pushes its right neighbor. Simultaneous left/right influences cancel when equal, leaving that domino upright.
Invariant: arr records net force accumulated at each position, and d marks positions already assigned a falling direction.
Edge cases: A domino receiving both directions in the same round has net zero and is not enqueued. The round-based processing is intended to prevent immediate directional conflicts from being resolved prematurely.
Complexity: Each position is discovered at most once after the initial forces, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine the final state of a row of dominoes after simultaneous pushes spread.
Idea: Accumulate rightward force in a left-to-right pass and leftward force in a right-to-left pass.
Technique and why it applies: Force decreases by one with each empty cell and resets at an opposing push. The difference of right and left forces determines R, L, or an upright dot.
Invariant: force[i] stores net influence after both directional scans.
Edge cases: Existing L and R dominoes reset the corresponding force scan, preventing forces from passing through them. Empty input returns an empty string.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and O(n) space for the force array.

Task and constraints: Count connected groups of strings that are equal or differ by one swap of two positions.
Idea: Build connected components implicitly by DFS, checking each unvisited string for similarity with the current one.
Technique and why it applies: If two anagrams differ at exactly two positions, swapping those characters can make them equal; identical strings are also similar because the mismatch count is zero.
Invariant: visited contains every string index reached in the current or previous component searches.
Edge cases: The code uses diff_count <= 2, which can classify strings with exactly one differing position as similar even though anagrams should differ at zero or two positions. This is only safe under the anagram input guarantee.
Complexity: Pairwise comparisons cost O(n²L) for n strings of length L, with O(n) visited storage and recursion.

Task and constraints: Count 3-by-3 magic squares embedded in a grid.
Idea: For each candidate 3-by-3 block, check all row sums, column sums, diagonal sums, and distinct values.
Technique and why it applies: A magic square's rows, columns, and diagonals share the same expected sum. The implementation uses k=3 and requires nine distinct values with minimum one.
Invariant: magic returns True only if each checked line has the expected sum and the values meet its distinctness/minimum tests.
Edge cases: It checks only minimum value and distinct count, not maximum value or that the values are exactly 1 through 9. For a 3-by-3 block, distinct positive integers with minimum one and sum 15 constraints imply the intended set only if all line checks also hold.
Complexity: Each block uses O(1) work for fixed k, giving O(RC) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether every room is reachable from room zero using keys found inside rooms.
Idea: Run breadth-first search starting from room zero and enqueue every key discovered in a visited room.
Technique and why it applies: A key to room v creates a directed edge from the current room to v. The visited set prevents repeatedly exploring the same room.
Invariant: visited_rooms contains all rooms whose keys have been processed.
Edge cases: collections is used without import in the snippet. Rooms is assumed nonempty because the queue begins with room zero.
Complexity: Each room and key edge is processed at most once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether all rooms can be reached from room zero through their keys.
Idea: Use iterative depth-first search with a stack and a set of discovered rooms.
Technique and why it applies: Each unseen key destination is added to lookup and pushed for later exploration. Reaching the total room count permits early success.
Invariant: lookup contains every room discovered so far, and stack contains discovered rooms awaiting expansion.
Edge cases: A single room returns True after processing because lookup size equals room count. The method assumes at least one room.
Complexity: Each room and key is processed once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Split a digit string into a Fibonacci-like sequence of at least three integers, each within the allowed integer bound.
Idea: Try possible first and second numbers, then recursively consume the exact decimal representation of each required next sum.
Technique and why it applies: Every later term is forced by the previous two. consume_tail checks whether that number begins the remaining suffix and continues if it does.
Invariant: current stores a valid Fibonacci prefix, and s is the unconsumed suffix that must match the next terms.
Edge cases: The bound is set to 2**31, although the common constraint is strictly less than 2**31; the check permits equality. Recursive depth can be linear in string length.
Complexity: Trying prefixes and recursive matching can be exponential in input length in the worst case, with O(n) recursion and sequence storage.

Task and constraints: Find a Fibonacci-like sequence of at least three integers that concatenates to S.
Idea: Enumerate first and second numbers, then greedily match each forced next sum against the remaining digits.
Technique and why it applies: The startswith helper parses digits until the number equals the required sum or exceeds it. Each successful match advances the suffix pointer by the matched length.
Invariant: fib is a valid prefix and k marks the first digit not yet consumed.
Edge cases: Leading zeros are handled by breaking after a zero-valued first or second number. MAX_INT is 2**31-1, correctly enforcing the signed 32-bit maximum.
Complexity: The two prefix loops and digit matching yield roughly O(n³) worst-case time, with O(n) sequence storage.

Task and constraints: Compare two strings after interpreting # as a backspace that deletes the preceding character.
Idea: Generate each final string backward without building it, skipping characters canceled by backspaces.
Technique and why it applies: debt counts pending deletions. A # increases debt; ordinary characters consume debt before being yielded. zip_longest compares the surviving characters from right to left.
Invariant: Each generator yields the final string's characters in reverse order.
Edge cases: zip_longest is used without import in the snippet, so execution fails unless provided externally. The code assumes # deletes one preceding character when available.
Complexity: Each character is processed once, giving O(n+m) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond generator state.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two strings are equal after applying all backspaces represented by #.
Idea: Scan both strings backward with generators that skip deleted characters, then compare the resulting character streams.
Technique and why it applies: Each # increments skip; ordinary characters reduce skip until an undeleted character can be yielded. zip_longest detects unequal remaining lengths as well as mismatches.
Invariant: findNextChar yields only characters that survive backspace processing, in reverse order.
Edge cases: Empty strings compare equal. zip_longest pads the shorter stream with None, so extra surviving characters force False.
Complexity: Each character is examined once, giving O(n+m) time and O(1) auxiliary state.

Task and constraints: Find the longest contiguous mountain: strictly increasing, then strictly decreasing, with both slopes nonempty.
Idea: Compute increasing-run lengths ending at each index and decreasing-run lengths starting there.
Technique and why it applies: A peak forms a mountain only when both lengths exceed one. Combining the two lengths and subtracting one avoids counting the peak twice.
Invariant: max_up[i] records the increasing run ending at i; max_down[i] records the decreasing run beginning at i.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return zero. Equal adjacent values break either slope and cannot belong to a strict mountain.
Complexity: Two scans take O(n) time and the arrays use O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the longest contiguous subarray that strictly rises and then strictly falls.
Idea: Track the current upward and downward slope lengths in one pass.
Technique and why it applies: A flat step or a rise after a descending phase resets the current mountain. Once both up_len and down_len are positive, their sum plus one gives its length.
Invariant: up_len counts consecutive increasing edges and down_len counts consecutive decreasing edges in the current candidate.
Edge cases: A mountain requires at least one edge in each direction, so monotone or flat arrays return zero. The reset condition restarts when a new ascent follows a descent.
Complexity: One pass uses O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
